title: Seating Arrangements That Promote Positive Academic and Behavioural Outcomes https://nasenjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9604.2008.00375.x
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 17, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page summarizes Wannarka and Ruhl's review of eight studies on classroom seating arrangements, asking whether rows or grouped desks better support positive academic and behavioral outcomes. The clearest finding is that students show more on-task behavior and less disruption when seated in rows during individual work, with the effect strongest for students already identified as disruptive. Group seating arrangements, by contrast, are more suited to interactive tasks that genuinely require collaboration. Barton's summary frames the core message as task-contingent: there is no single best seating arrangement, and teachers should match the layout to the nature of the activity rather than adopt one default configuration. The review also flags open questions, including how seating affects older students and the quality, not just the quantity, of work produced under different arrangements.
points: Rows outperform groups for individual, independent work, especially for students already identified as behaviorally disruptive, because rows make off-task behavior more visible and interaction less convenient.
Group and cluster seating should be reserved for genuinely interactive tasks like brainstorming or discussion, where the format's collaborative benefits actually apply.
There is no single best seating arrangement for all tasks; the nature of the activity, not habit or classroom aesthetics, should dictate the layout.
More research is needed on seating effects for students older than 15 and on how arrangement affects the quality, not just the quantity, of student work.
quotes: This study examines the relationship between classroom seating arrangements and student behavior, specifically focusing on whether rows or groups of desks are more effective for promoting positive academic and behavioral outcomes.
Students exhibit more on-task behavior and less disruptive behavior when seated in rows during individual tasks, particularly students who are identified as being more disruptive.
Rows make it inconvenient for students to interact with each other and make off-task behavior more obvious to the teacher.

Rows are particularly effective for students who exhibit disruptive behavior. Research has consistently shown that rows are superior in minimizing disruptive behavior and maximizing on-task behavior during individual activities.

There is no single classroom seating arrangement that promotes positive behavioural and academic outcomes for all tasks, because the available research clearly indicates that the nature (i.e., interactive versus independent) of the task should dictate the arrangement.
